Patient safety in healthcare is a critical issue that was spotlighted by the Institute of Medicine's landmark report, "To Err is Human." In addition to proper staffing levels, there are other resources that healthcare facilities can leverage to improve safety.  

### Why is it important?

Patient safety issues that can occur are wide-ranging and can take the form of falls, pressure ulcers, medication errors, hospital acquired infections, post-surgical infections, wrong-site surgeries, and death. The general resources outlined on the next page can help address many of these safety issues.   

In the article, "5 Must-Have Resources for Patient Safety in Hospitals," Lori Pilla outlines several resources hospitals and clinics can use to improve patient safety. **Several of these suggestions are summarized below:**
 
- **Chair and Bed Protection**  
Falls have become so prevalent that the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid will no longer reimburse for fall-related injuries. Resources designed to reduce falls or injuries associated with falls include:
>- Fall risk indicators
>- Bed/chair exit alarms
>- Floor cushions and mats
>- Hip protectors
>- Side rail protectors

- **Resources to Prevent Bloodstream Infections**  
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 41,000 patients per year develop central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSIs). Researchers have found that using maximal sterile barrier (MSB) precautions during central venous catheter (CVC) placement reduces the risk of CLABSIs. The CVC inserter should wear a mask and cap, a sterile gown and sterile gloves. A head-to-toe sterile drape should also be placed over the patient during the placement/exchange of a catheter. Hospitals can also purchase either antimicrobial or antiseptic-impregnated catheters. Finally, many providers even choose to add disinfection cap systems, designed for needle-free valves, to the end of the IV tubing

- **Medication-Labeling Systems**  
Medication errors result in 7,000 deaths every year, and the FDA reports that 50 percent of reported medications errors involve discrepancy in naming, labeling or packaging. There are now medication labelling systems specifically designed to work with hospital, pharmacy and laboratory software. They can produce bar coded, blank and combination labels in a wide range of sizes, formats, materials and adhesives as each hospital prefers. Importantly, they can also produce instructional and warning labels that save patients and caregivers from a potentially dangerous error. 

- **Continuing Education**  
As the advances in safety supplies indicate, best practices are going to evolve and compliance requirements will change along with them. Hospital staff need continuing education and access to the latest resources in order to provide top quality care and maintain patient safety. Healthcare organizations must encourage clinicians to stay up-to-date with new innovations, standards and thought leadership.  You do not want to look back on a safety incident thinking, "We didn't know," or "We should have purchased ____." Unfortunately, the healthcare world has had to learn from mistakes and knowledge gaps that shape our current safety practices. Fortunately, you can establish practices and provide resources to prevent history from repeating itself.

- **Helpful Technology**  
Implementing proven technology can also improve patient safety. According to a technology review by Alotaibi and Federico in 2017, the authors concluded that there is substantial evidence that implementing an electronic medical record reduces medical errors and improves patient's safety. Furthermore, they found that computerized physician order entry and CDS are probably one of the most beneficial health information technologies for improving patient safety. Finally, ADC systems and PDMS seem to improve patient safety in critical care settings.

>Sources:

>Pilla, L. 5 Must-Have Resources for Patient Safety in Hospital
